newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish talks under new threat - Protestant leader.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish talks under new threat - Protestant leader.

text.p: Northern Irish peace talks appeared to be under a new threat late on Wednesday after a Protestant politician said that a second group of Protestant guerrillas had grown dissatisfied with the lack of progress.

David Ervine of the Progressive Unionist Party said that he expected prisoners among the party's guerrilla wing, the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), to issue a statement next week about the talks, Britain's Press Association news agency reported.

Last week, 400 prisoners from the UDA Protestant guerrilla group, who are seen as underground leaders of the pro-British "Loyalists", declared a vote of no-confidence in the peace talks, jointly sponsored by Britain and Ireland.
"You can be assured if the UDA are unhappy then the UVF are also unhappy. My understanding is that they will say something next week," Ervine said.

"It's my belief that within the next week or fortnight that the political process will collapse...leaving us with the vacuum that will undoubtedly be filled with violence from both sides," he told a fringe meeting at the annual conference of Britain's opposition Labour Party.
The UVF and the UDA are the two main Protestant guerrilla groups in Northern Ireland fighting to maintain British rule of the province.
Their political leaders have been allowed into the peace talks, chaired by George Mitchell of the United States, because the guerrillas have observed a ceasefire for two years.
Sinn Fein, the political wing of the laregly Roman Catholic Irish Republican Army, has been barred from the talks until the guerrillas resume a 17-month ceasefire they abandoned in February.
The talks, which resumed on Monday after a summer recess, already appeared to be precarious after the withdrawal of support by the UDA leaders.
They were further undermined by accusations from Protestant politicians that London and Dublin are caving in to IRA guerrillas campaigning for an end to British rule of the province.

Protestant parties demanding that the IRA scrap its arms before being given a seat at the talks say they fear that the issue of guerrillas surrendering weapons may be sidelined so that Sinn Fein can be eased into the talks.
